input:
Case
This proposal sets out the case for a rooftop solar installation and seeks approval to move forward to the detailed design stage. This is not a request for approval to construct the installation itself, and no commitment to build should be inferred from the approval that is being requested at this point. The fundamental idea is simple: photovoltaic modules on the roof generate electricity where it is used, and every unit generated displaces a unit the site would otherwise purchase from the grid. At present, the roof carries no plant and earns nothing; fitted with modules, that same area becomes a productive generation asset, without taking up land or floor space that operations depend on. Generation from the array peaks in the middle of the day, precisely when site demand for lighting, ventilation and process services is also at its daily height, so a large share of the output is consumed on site as it is produced rather than exported at a lower value. Purchased electricity, by contrast, represents a continuing operating cost whose price the site does not control. Generation behind the meter reduces the volume exposed to that price, and this reduction endures for the entire life of the installation. It should be emphasised that the case does not rest on the array supplying the whole site: the array offsets part of the purchased volume, while the grid remains the source for the balance and for all hours of darkness. What has not been established at this stage is the roof itself. The capacity of the structure to carry the modules and their mounting loads, the orientation and pitch of the available slopes, the shading cast by plant on and around the roof, and the remaining life of the roof covering all bear directly on whether the installation is sound, and none of these questions is settled by the information behind this proposal. The detailed design will settle each point in turn. The appraisal presented in the costs section therefore tests a pre-design capital figure against the horizon over which the installation would operate, and the decision requested simply asks for the design work that will turn an outline case into a fully priced and thoroughly checked proposal.

Costs
The capital cost of the proposed installation is $1075k. This figure covers the photovoltaic modules, the inverters, the mounting system and its fixings, the cabling and switchgear, the grid connection works, and the labour of installation. This is a pre-design figure. No supplier has yet priced a final layout, the inverter selection is not fixed, and the allowance for the grid connection rests on the connection route that the detailed design will confirm with the network operator; each of these items could move the outturn cost in either direction. Running costs over the life of the installation are small beside the capital figure and are confined to cleaning of the module surfaces, periodic inspection of the mounting and electrical connections, and the monitoring service that reports generation and faults. The modules have no fuel cost and no moving parts. Inverters, however, have a shorter service life than modules, and a replacement will fall inside the appraisal horizon on the lives stated by the manufacturers; the detailed design will fix the inverter count and rating, and the appraisal will then carry a replacement allowance at the appropriate point in the horizon. Two costs are excluded from the capital figure, because neither can be priced before the design work is done: structural strengthening of the roof, should the survey show that the existing structure cannot carry the array, and any loss of use of the areas below the roof while installation proceeds overhead. The appraisal horizon is 10 years. The benefit side of the appraisal is the generation predicted by the detailed design, valued as displaced purchases at the tariff the site pays, with module output degrading year by year at the rate the design adopts. Costs and benefits are compared over the same horizon, and the appraisal will be re-run on the firmed figures when the detailed design reports, before any request to construct is made.

Schedule
Work starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design itself, encompassing the roof survey and structural check, the array layout, the electrical design, and the connection application to the network operator, whose terms can govern the overall programme if the connection works turn out to be extensive. Procurement follows the design; modules, inverters and mounting are standard items with order lead times that the design programme will state, and no order will be placed before the design is issued. Installation then follows procurement and is sequenced slope by slope, so that only part of the roof is under work at any given time, the building below stays weather-tight at the end of each stage, and operations under the roof can continue with agreed exclusions around the working area. Commissioning closes the sequence: protection settings and metering are agreed with the network operator, the installation is tested and energised, and generation is handed over to the site with its monitoring in place. No contractor is named at this stage. The installation contractor will be appointed after the detailed design, under the procurement route that the design documents set out, and it is the design programme, rather than this proposal, that will carry the dates for each stage measured from the start.

Decision requested
In conclusion, the decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, and nothing further. The design will return a surveyed layout with a generation prediction the site can rely on, a structural statement for the roof, connection terms agreed in principle with the network operator, and a capital cost firm enough to appraise the installation as an investment. Construction is a separate decision, to be taken on the basis of those deliverables by the same route as this one. Approval of the design stage commits the site to the design fee and to no other spend: if the structural statement is adverse, if the connection terms are onerous, or if the firmed cost destroys the case set out above, the project simply stops at that point and the work done remains as a record of why. The appraisal will then be re-run on the firmed figures, and a construction request will be put forward only if the case survives it.
